ARCIL - Q1FY27 | Concall Insights

Financial Highlights
•Q1 revenue from operations INR 274 cr, +128% YoY; total income INR 276 cr, +115% YoY
•Fee and other income more than doubled to INR 118 cr on larger AUM and higher resolution
•Recovery of amounts written off earlier INR 120 cr
•PBT INR 192 cr, +106% YoY; PAT INR 143 cr, +107% YoY; PAT margin 52% of total income
•Q1 profit was about 35% of last year’s full-year profit; management asked for a full-year read because acquisitions are seasonal and corporate recoveries are chunky

Recoveries 
•Total recoveries INR 1,066 cr vs INR 425 cr in Q1 FY26, +151%
•Cumulative SR redemption 52.5% vs 50.8% in March 2026
•Corporate book about INR 13,000 cr; resolutions are event-based (settlements, court orders, asset sales) and will not repeat evenly
•Historical recovery has been 21–25% of opening AUM every year
•Write-backs are a recurring but lumpy line: INR 288 cr in FY24, INR 100 cr in FY25, INR 66 cr in FY26; expected to continue for a few years and then fade as system write-offs have already slowed

AUM 
•AUM INR 19,574 cr as on 30 June 2026, +16% YoY
•Dues under management INR 1.40 lakh cr, +20% YoY
•AUM grew from INR 15,230 cr in March 2024 to INR 20,150 cr in March 2026, about 15% a year; own investment in that AUM grew about 26% a year
•Industry AUM share rose from 11% to 15% over two years
•Share of new industry acquisitions: 6% in FY24, 10% in FY25, 17% in FY26; FY26 acquisitions close to INR 6,000 cr
•Q1 FY27 acquisitions INR 353 cr, with INR 143 cr of own capital; about INR 150 cr below Q1 FY26 and about 2.5% of FY26 full-year acquisitions
•Pipeline called encouraging; acquisitions expected to build through the year; no quarterly acquisition number given because Q2 results were not yet out
•Assets bought at about 26% of dues, held at 26–27% every year; current AUM is about 14% of the INR 1.4 lakh cr of dues managed

Strategy
•No numeric AUM or profit guidance
•Intent is to keep acquiring and resolving; growing AUM by not resolving is not the model
•Resolution run-rate framed at 20–25% of opening AUM
•Buy with discipline, resolve with urgency, deploy capital for returns
•Collection-as-a-service to be offered to banks and NBFCs on the retail platform
•Last-mile funding up to 25% of an acquired loan can be provided to support a turnaround

Income Quality
•Income is management fees, recovery incentives, SR investment returns, upside on full redemption, interest, write-backs and mark-to-market
•Finance cost INR 25 cr vs INR 3.2 cr; borrowings were raised from H2 FY26 and those acquisitions have not yet fully earned
•Initial provision INR 22 cr on receivables expected to be realised and reversed near term

Balance Sheet
•Net worth INR 3,222 cr; net own funds INR 2,792 cr; CRAR 72.5%
•Borrowings INR 1,100 cr vs INR 1,200 cr in March; debt to equity 0.34x
•Own SR investment about INR 4,200 cr, roughly 22% of AUM
•Sequential debt decline is seasonal; lines are drawn mainly for year-end acquisitions and repaid as resolutions come in
•Expect to draw down again and marginally lift leverage as the H2 pipeline converts; capacity to fund acquisitions called ample

Industry
•CRISIL stressed pool (SMA, NPA and written-off) across banks and NBFCs about INR 23–24 lakh cr; written-off about INR 12 lakh cr
•Pool has been rising about INR 1 lakh cr a year; ARCs still take under 10%
•SMA can now be bought before NPA; SMA was about 30% of new ARC acquisitions in FY25 vs about 14% in FY24
•Industry recovery rates cited as having moved from about 35% to about 85%; driver is a better economy and real-estate assets stressed four to five years ago now redeeming SRs
•Higher ARC share attributed to lenders freeing capital and bandwidth, and to ARCs having the full resolution toolkit
•Retail platform covers 3.29 million borrowers, with scorecards, skip tracing, segmentation, automated settlement and digital payments

🏭 MTAR Technologies – ESG Rating 

ESG means how well a company performs in three areas:

- E – Environmental: How the company manages pollution, energy, waste, etc.
- S – Social: Employee safety, welfare, community, etc.
- G – Governance: Management quality, transparency, rules and ethics.

📊 What happened?

- CRISIL ESG Ratings & Analytics gave MTAR Technologies an ESG rating of 63.
- CRISIL placed the company in the “Strong” category.
- Rating date: 6 October 2026.
- The assessment was based on publicly available FY26 information.
- MTAR did not directly engage CRISIL for this assessment.

🟢 Why is this useful for investors?

A strong ESG rating can indicate that the company has relatively good practices around:

Environment + Employees/Society + Corporate Governance.

This can be useful because large institutional investors increasingly consider ESG factors when evaluating companies.

⚠️ Important point

ESG rating is not the same as financial performance.

It does not automatically mean:

- Higher profit
- Higher share price
- Better valuation
- Higher future returns

For MTAR, investors should still check revenue growth, order book, EBITDA margin, PAT, debt, cash flow and ROCE.

🎯 Simple conclusion

👉 MTAR receiving a CRISIL ESG 63 “Strong” rating is a positive non-financial development.

“MTAR has received a strong score for its environmental, social and governance practices, but investors should evaluate this together with the company's financial performance.”

AIM Research has launched the 'Top Sovereign Cloud Infrastructure Providers in India PeMa Quadrant 2026', assessing 13 providers on Market Penetration and Technology Maturity as the regulatory landscape reshapes how Indian enterprises evaluate cloud.

For a decade, cloud decisions rested on price, features and proximity. The DPDP Act, RBI localisation rules, SEBI and IRDAI cloud frameworks, MeitY empanelment and the IndiaAI Mission have changed what the decision rests on, and sovereign cloud is the commercial answer. 

The study treats sovereignty as broader than keeping workloads inside national borders, reading it across where data, backups, logs and telemetry actually reside, who operates the environment and holds privileged access, which legal system governs the contracting entity, where the control plane runs and who holds the encryption keys. The control plane carries the most weight, because software that configures, monitors and can suspend an environment can be operated from outside the country even when every server sits inside it.

Demand is arriving along two lines, with government bodies and regulated enterprises evaluating cloud as part of their risk and control architecture, while AI-led buyers start from GPU availability, price per GPU-hour and deployment speed. The evidence both are looking for is already running across national and citizen-scale platforms, regulated production workloads in banking and insurance, air-gapped environments and in-country disaster recovery across separate seismic zones.

If GPUs are so valuable, why don't companies just buy them instead of renting from E2E or ESDS?

This is probably one of the most important questions to understand behind the GPU cloud story.

At first it sounds simple.

If a company needs GPUs, why not just buy them and build its own infrastructure?

Because buying the GPU is only the first step.

First problem is availability.

High end GPUs are expensive and getting large quantities on time can itself be difficult.

But assume the company manages to buy them.

Now the real work starts.

You need data centre space.

Power.

Cooling.

Networking.

Storage.

GPU servers.

Drivers.

CUDA stack.

Cluster management.

Monitoring.

Security.

Backups.

And people who know how to maintain all of this.

Then comes an even bigger problem.

What happens when something fails?

Suppose a bank is running an important AI service.

A GPU fails.

A node goes down.

Networking breaks.

Storage becomes unavailable.

If the infrastructure is not designed properly, the entire service can stop.

That is why companies need things like

Fault tolerance

Redundancy

Failure handling

Load balancing

Monitoring

High availability

Automatic recovery

All of this becomes an additional burden for a company whose main business may be banking, insurance, healthcare or manufacturing.

They don't necessarily want to become data centre and GPU infrastructure experts.

This is where companies like E2E Networks and ESDS come in.

Instead of the customer buying and maintaining the entire GPU infrastructure, they can rent the compute.

E2E or ESDS handles much of the infrastructure burden.

The customer can focus more on building the AI application.

So instead of thinking

Why would anyone rent a GPU?

I think the better question is

Why would every company want to build and maintain its own GPU infrastructure?

There is also flexibility.

A company may need 20 GPUs today.

100 GPUs during a training job.

Then only 10 GPUs after the model goes into production.

If they buy everything for peak demand, a lot of expensive hardware can remain underutilised later.

Renting makes that easier.

But this does not mean renting is always better.

If a very large company has predictable GPU demand and very high utilisation for years, owning its own infrastructure can eventually become cheaper.

That is why hyperscalers and very large AI companies build their own infrastructure.

But for a huge number of enterprises, startups and BFSI companies, renting removes a lot of complexity.

And that is the real value companies like E2E Networks and ESDS are trying to sell.

Not just GPUs.

Reliable access to GPU compute without the customer having to build everything around it.

Adani Enterprises: net invested ₹8,379 crore; committed ₹9,65,000 crore**; targeted capacity 5 GW

*Reliance figure excludes the 168MW data centre in partnership with Meta; **committed figures include other sectors such as renewable energy and AI

The Rivals
Tata Group: has so far invested at least ₹1,447 crore through two companies

Tata Communications has invested about ₹1,247 crore in STT Global Data Centres since 2016; STT has an operational capacity of over 400 MW

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has invested at least ₹200 crore in HyperVault Data Centres Pvt Ltd, its data centre venture set up with private equity firm TPG in 2025; TCS is the newest entrant

Airtel's Nxtra was established in 2013, giving it a head start of several years over others

Reliance's Digital Connexion was formed in 2023

The differing timelines partly explain the gap in cumulative investment, even as all four are now stepping up plans to capture AI-driven demand

Capacity Targets

Ayush Rungta (Deloitte India): each conglomerate has deep pockets; most are likely to infuse more capital as demand picks up, and the inflection point from a demand perspective should happen soon, after which more money will be pumped in

Analysts said conglomerates might edge out standalone operators

Core Theme 
Adani has built a clear early lead in India's data centre race, with about ₹8,379 crore invested in AdaniConneX and a 5 GW target, nearly double the combined spend of Airtel, Reliance and Tata; with each rival entering at a different time and all now ramping up on AI-driven demand, analysts expect deep-pocketed conglomerates to pour in more capital and potentially edge out standalone operators, though underutilisation risk remains unless hyperscaler-backed demand materialises.
